title: India's Big Moment at Cannes 2026 — Regional Cinema Takes the Global Stage
excerpt: Seven Indian films — in Punjabi, Malayalam, Assamese, and Kannada — are screening at the 79th Cannes Film Festival, marking a watershed moment for non-Hindi Indian cinema on the world stage.
body:
Something extraordinary is happening on the French Riviera right now — and it's not just Alia Bhatt's pastel corset gown breaking the internet.

At the 79th Cannes Film Festival, India isn't whispering from the margins. It's commanding the room. Seven Indian films are screening across sections this year, and here's the part that should make every desi cinephile's heart sing: nearly all of them are in regional languages. Punjabi. Malayalam. Assamese. Bodo. Kannada. This isn't Bollywood's show anymore. This is *India's* show.

## The Films That Got the Golden Ticket

**Chardikala**, a Punjabi-language drama starring Ammy Virk, is perhaps the biggest headline-grabber — a full Punjabi film competing at Cannes is the kind of sentence that would've sounded absurd even five years ago. Alongside it, **Balan: The Boy** represents Malayalam cinema's relentless march onto the world stage, while FTII's **Shadows of the Moonless Night**, another Punjabi short film, proves that India's film schools are producing world-class talent.

Then there's the restoration crowd going wild over **Amma Ariyan** (1986), John Abraham's legendary Malayalam classic, getting the Cannes Classics treatment — a film many NRIs have only ever heard about from their parents now preserved for global audiences.

But the real sleeper story? **Kenny Basumatary's "My Three Sisters"**, an Assamese-Bodo language film screening at the Marché du Film. Northeast Indian cinema at Cannes. Let that sink in.

**Lakadbaggha 2: The Monkey Business** and the Hindi-Kannada hybrid **September 21** round out the official selections, while documentarian Siddharth Sinha's **Spirit of the Wildflower** adds to the non-fiction contingent.

## India's Business Takeover

It's not just art — it's commerce. The **IMPPA pavilion** is back at Palais-1 (Booth 21.05) for its third consecutive year, showcasing over 35 films to international buyers. This is where deals get done, where a Marathi film finds a German distributor, where a Tamil thriller gets picked up for a Korean remake.

Speaking of Marathi: the **Abhijat OTT platform** launched at the Bharat Pavilion specifically targeting the global Marathi diaspora. If you're a Marathi-speaking NRI who's been starving for content in your mother tongue, this one's for you.

Meanwhile, **Studio PictureWorks** made waves by launching the first-ever Indian production slate at Cannes — including a Hindi remake of a French film (meta, given the setting) and a Kannada feature. Gujarat's **Chanda Patel** debuted with "Tera Mera Nata," and **Aushim Khetarpal's** "Children of God" screened to festival audiences.

## The Red Carpet Moment

No Cannes dispatch is complete without fashion, and Alia Bhatt delivered. Her pastel corset gown lit up every South Asian WhatsApp group from Jersey City to Southall. When trolls came for her (as they always do), Sonu Sood and Ameesha Patel were quick to shut it down — a rare moment of Bollywood solidarity that felt genuinely sweet.

https://www.instagram.com/aliaabhatt/

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

Here's the thing that makes this year different. For decades, "Indian cinema at Cannes" meant one thing: will a Bollywood A-lister walk the red carpet? The conversation was about glamour, not craft. About Hindi, not Haryanvi.

2026 has flipped that script entirely. When a Punjabi film, an Assamese-Bodo film, and a restored Malayalam classic all screen at the same festival — with an entire OTT platform launching for the Marathi diaspora — the message is unmistakable: Indian cinema's global future is multilingual.

For NRIs, this is personal. These aren't just "foreign films" winning festival cred. These are the languages of our grandparents, the stories from our hometowns, the cultures we've been trying to keep alive in our kids. And now they're on the biggest cinema stage in the world.

Park Chan-wook's jury will hand out prizes on May 23. But India has already won something bigger: proof that the world is finally ready for the full, gorgeous, chaotic diversity of Indian storytelling.

*The 79th Cannes Film Festival runs through May 23, 2026. Most of these films will eventually hit OTT platforms accessible internationally — we'll update streaming availability as it's announced.*
